components.title: Mapping Natural Language Requirements to Interface Contracts
components.teaches: Students will learn how to systematically convert informal, natural-language module requirements into structured interface contracts. The instructor demonstrates transforming ambiguous functional statements into unambiguous method signatures with specific parameters, return types, and exceptions. Students evaluate how precise specification bounds prevent runtime errors during code generation.

components.title: Specifying Preconditions, Postconditions, and Invariants
components.teaches: Students will formulate explicit invariants, preconditions, and postconditions for every public method in a target module using contract specification frameworks. They will construct concrete validation constraints for input parameters and standard return states. This ensures AI codegen tools generate implementation logic that strictly adheres to the specified contract.

components.title: Automated Test Generation from Executable Specifications
components.teaches: Students will observe how spec-driven frameworks automatically synthesize property-based tests and mock servers directly from specification definitions. The demonstration shows running executable specs against sample code to verify whether public methods conform to defined constraints. Students learn to interpret automated test failures resulting from specification violations.

components.title: Translating Complex Module Requirements into Executable Specifications
components.teaches: Students will follow a step-by-step translation of a multi-method business module's requirements into a complete, executable specification file. The worked example walks through defining request validation, error states, and public interface expectations for each method. Students see how to verify that every requirement maps directly to an executable check.

components.title: Mitigating Spec Drift and Handling Edge Cases
components.teaches: Students will analyze techniques for maintaining synchronization between evolving executable specifications and generated code over time. They will evaluate trade-offs in spec granularity, identifying when over-specifying hinders LLM code generation flexibility versus under-specifying causing contract breaches. Students discuss strategies to handle edge-case error scenarios within the spec framework.

video.description:
As AI coding agents automate syntax writing, human software engineering is shifting from writing code by hand to architecting precise technical specifications. Without unambiguous specs, autonomous agents waste cycles, hallucinate dependencies, and drift off-target.

This is a comprehensive look at Spec-Driven Development (SDD): structuring specification artifacts, eliminating ambiguity for AI agents, building executable specs, and setting up automated test rails.

WHAT YOU GET OUT OF IT - The paradigm shift from manual coding to specification architecture - The 4 essential SDD artifacts: REQUIREMENTS.md, OpenAPI, AGENTS.md, and TESTS.md - How to draft unambiguous specs that eliminate agent

video.description:
Vibe coding is fast, but it often produces code that doesn't match what you asked for. Spec-driven development is the disciplined alternative: write a clear markdown spec defining what to build, and let your coding agent implement it.

Earn your certificate here: https://bit.ly/4hmJc2K

You'll learn to:
- Write a project constitution defining mission, tech stack, and roadmap
- Plan, implement, and validate features using a spec as the agent's guide
- Introduce SDD to a legacy codebase
- Package your workflow into an agent skill that's portable across agents and IDEs

Spec-Driven Development with Coding Agents is built in partnership with JetBrains and taught by Paul Everitt, Developer Advoca

video.description:
Your OpenAPI specification passes Spectral, Redocly or Vacuum...

But is it actually executable?

Traditional OpenAPI linters focus on syntax, style and structural correctness. They tell you whether your specification is valid.

Specmatic goes a step further.

It validates whether your OpenAPI specification is semantically correct, internally consistent and actually executable.

In this video you'll see:

✅ Why syntactically valid OpenAPI specs can still fail at runtime
✅ Real examples that traditional linters miss
✅ A comparison of Spectral, Redocly, Vacuum and Specmatic
✅ How Specmatic detects semantic and runtime inconsistencies
✅ Enterprise API governance features including Maturity Leve
